title: Kinds of Documentary
objective: After this level you can tell expository, observational and participatory documentaries apart and say what each one is best at.
summary: Nichols's modes: expository films argue with narration, observational films watch quietly, and participatory films put the filmmaker in the scene.

cards.headline: Three documentaries about one strike. Why do they feel so different?
cards.body: One explains it with a confident narrator. One just watches the picket line. One has the filmmaker arguing with the boss on camera. All three are documentaries. They're just different kinds.

cards.headline: Expository: the film argues
cards.body: In Introduction to Documentary (2001), Bill Nichols identified six modes of documentary; a film usually has one dominant mode but can mix them. Expository films argue a point, often through an authoritative "voice-of-God" narrator, using images as evidence. Night Mail (1936), from John Grierson, is a classic. Level 19's Grierson was the man who first called Flaherty's work documentary.

cards.headline: Observational: the film watches
cards.body: Observational documentaries use an unobtrusive camera and minimal intervention: no narration, no interviews. D. A. Pennebaker's Don't Look Back (1967) is an example. It's best at letting you watch events unfold and judge for yourself. The catch: you only see what was filmed and kept.

cards.headline: Participatory: the filmmaker joins in
cards.body: In participatory documentaries the filmmaker appears on camera and interviews people, admitting that their presence shapes events, as in Michael Moore's Roger & Me (1989). Britannica sums up the split: direct cinema observed like a fly on the wall, while cinéma vérité participated like a fly in the soup. It's best at showing how people respond when questioned.

questions.prompt: Match each documentary mode with its example film.
questions.explanation: Night Mail is a classic expository documentary, Don't Look Back is observational, and Michael Moore's Roger & Me is participatory.

questions.prompt: A new film follows a band on tour with no narrator and no interviews, just a quiet camera. Which mode is it, and what is it best at?

options.label: Expository: best at arguing a clear point
options.rationale: It has no narrator making an argument.

options.label: Observational: best at letting you watch events unfold
Participatory: best at showing people's reactions to the filmmaker
options.rationale: The filmmaker never appears or asks questions.

options.label: It isn't a documentary at all

questions.explanation: An unobtrusive camera with no narration or interviews is the observational mode.

questions.prompt: Nanook of the North built a cut-away igloo and staged a seal hunt. Which documentary mode's ideal does that break most clearly?

options.label: Observational, which aims for minimal intervention
Expository, which forbids images as evidence
options.rationale: Expository films use images as evidence.

options.label: Participatory, which forbids the filmmaker appearing
options.rationale: Participatory films put the filmmaker on camera.

options.label: None: staging is the goal of every mode
options.rationale: Observational films aim to intervene as little as possible.

questions.explanation: Building sets and staging events is heavy intervention, the opposite of the observational ideal.
